cells.tense: Fairness moves through you now without the arithmetic, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.act: let the old form go so the next one can come
cells.ask: Name one arrangement between you and another that has run its course. Say it's finished, don't reopen it, and let whatever comes next take shape without your design.
cells.core:
Under the surface of a thing, you can see an arrangement has gone out of true before anyone says a word. You don't need to count what each side gave; the sense of what's fair sits quiet in you, and you can act from it without a ledger.

So name one arrangement — a split, a standing turn, a way you've both done it since before either of you could say why — and say it's finished. Don't reopen it. What comes next doesn't have to be designed by you; the space can stay open a while and you can watch what arrives. The exchange runs lighter for the room you make, and nobody has to keep score to feel it.
cells.sheetLine: You can see it's out of true before anyone says it.
cells.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
cells.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars

cells.tense: You are running the numbers on a fairness that hasn't happened yet.
cells.act: keep it at its real size when you are asked to shrink it
cells.ask: Choose a debt you've been carrying tallies on. Put the tally where you can see it and add no lines to it, whatever anyone asks you to feel about its size.
cells.core:
The pattern under an exchange is what you read, and the reading has turned into tracking. Who gave what, when, how much — the glance you used to take has become a record, and the people in the exchange can feel the record even when it stays in your hands. The fairness didn't go anywhere. The counting is standing in front of it.

Choose a debt you've been carrying tallies on and hold it at the size it actually is. Add no lines. When someone asks you to shrink it or make it bigger, keep it where it sits. The weight stays what it is, and the exchange stops needing a bookkeeper. What you were tracking will hold without the tallying.
cells.sheetLine: The pattern got a ledger, and the ledger got you.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed a long time ago.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Alone today with a page, put something you are owed and have not asked for onto it. Nothing more than that. Same again tomorrow.
cells.core:
What fair would look like is visible to you — clearly enough that you know it isn't what's happening. Where things got set right before, asking came to feel expensive, and asking has gone quiet. You take what comes and call it enough. The sense of what's owed hasn't stopped running in you.

Alone with a page today, put something you're owed and haven't asked for onto it. Don't ask yet. Tomorrow, the same. The practice stays small on purpose. It keeps what you already see in your own hand until asking costs less, and nothing out there has to change this week. The page fills. Your hand gets steadier.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what's fair and you've stopped asking.
cells.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level

cells.tense: You are weighing something this moment, pen down, and don't know the scale is in your hand.
cells.act: notice what you already know before you reason about it
cells.ask: The situation that's been nagging you — put your first read of it onto paper in a line, before you argue with yourself over it. One line. Then go about the day.
cells.core:
Something in an exchange has been running through you as a tally — who did what, what it cost, what they still owe. If someone asked, you'd say you weren't keeping score. The score is being kept, in your own hand, and the counting is the part you haven't looked at.

Before you reason about it, put your first read of the nagging situation onto paper. One line, no argument under it. You saw the imbalance before you could explain it; let that line stay and go about your day. The tally gets its edge back as a perception, which is what it was before it turned into arithmetic. The hand and the scale are the same hand.
cells.sheetLine: The tally is yours, and the hand writing it is yours.
cells.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
cells.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person is currently in an unfair situation or owes themselves a claim — the draw only says fairness runs naturally in them; the reader could rightly say 'nobody is owed anything right now.' The ask survives being wrong: releasing one arrangement that has gone stale teaches the shape of fair recalibration even if nothing is out of joint. The sentence that serves me more than them: 'you can feel it fully and still weigh it fairly' — too neat, cut it. In Too Little I say the person tolerates unfair treatment without naming what past made fairness feel dangerous. In Unacknowledged I say the tallying is theirs while claiming they don't know it — that is the card's own signature, not my invention.
